lead: A battery label is a promise about charge and current. Ampere-hour (Ah) says how much charge it stores; reserve capacity says how long it can run essential loads; cold cranking amps (CCA) says how much current it can push into a cold engine. Tests compare that promise with the battery's real condition. Ratings guide battery selection; tests decide replacement. You meet them at every service bay, battery shop and vehicle assembly line.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.4 for cell construction and discharge.

blocks.text: Ampere-hour (Ah) is stored charge. A 60 Ah battery at the 20 h rate can deliver 60 Ah when discharged over 20 h. The test current is constant.

blocks.where: I is constant current in A; t is discharge time in h; Ah is ampere-hour capacity.

blocks.text: At the 20 h rate, I = Ah ÷ 20 h. So 60 Ah gives 3 A. The test ends at 10.5 V (1.75 V per cell) at a stated temperature, usually about 25 °C. A battery discharged faster gives fewer ampere-hours, because the acid cannot reach the inner pores of the plates in time, so a rating always names its rate.

Reserve capacity (RC) is the time in minutes a fully charged battery at about 25 °C can supply 25 A before terminal voltage falls to 10.5 V. It answers: if the alternator fails, how long will lights and wipers run?

Cold cranking amps (CCA) is the current a battery can deliver at −18 °C for 30 s while keeping at least 7.2 V across its terminals (the SAE definition). Cranking amps (CA) uses the same 30 s and 7.2 V, but at 0 °C. European and Japanese standards use other times and end voltages, so compare ratings measured to the same standard.
Ah is not starting current. A high-Ah battery may have low CCA; a small, high-CCA battery may have modest Ah. Read both.

head: Rating
Unit
Test condition
rows: Constant current for 20 h to 10.5 V, about 25 °C

blocks.text: Open-circuit voltage (OCV) is measured after the battery rests, with no load. A full 12 V battery reads about 12.6 V to 12.8 V, 12.2 V about half charge, and 12.0 V about a quarter charge; below roughly 11.9 V it is deeply discharged.
A hydrometer measures specific gravity (SG) of the electrolyte. Full is about 1.265; 1.120 is nearly empty. Correct for temperature. Sealed batteries have no caps, so use OCV or a conductance tester.

items: Load test: apply half the CCA or three times the Ah for 15 s; voltage should stay above about 9.6 V at room temperature.
Conductance test: inject a small AC signal and read the estimated CCA; fast, safe and needs no full discharge.
Charging-system test: run the engine at fast idle and measure the voltage across the battery terminals; about 13.8 V to 14.4 V shows the alternator is charging.

blocks.text: Safety: a charging battery makes hydrogen gas, which explodes with a spark. Wear eye protection, keep flames away, and vent the area. Acid burns skin. Disconnect the negative terminal first and reconnect it last.

A load test heats the battery; let it rest before repeating. A conductance test can pass a battery that later fails under real cold cranking, so use it as a quick screen, not a guarantee. The charging circuit itself is covered in Chapter 1.6.

A maintenance-free battery limits water loss so it needs no periodic topping-up. Flooded maintenance-free types are vented through small vents. Only valve-regulated types (AGM, gel) carry a pressure-relief valve.

Lead-calcium grids replace the antimony of conventional grids with calcium (hybrid designs keep a little antimony in one plate). Calcium reduces gassing and self-discharge, so less water is lost. Calcium also makes the battery less tolerant of deep discharge.

VRLA means valve-regulated lead-acid. The valve releases gas only if pressure rises too far. In absorbed glass mat (AGM), a glass mat holds the electrolyte like a sponge, so it cannot spill. Oxygen made at the positive plate diffuses to the negative plate and recombines to water. This gas recombination keeps water inside.

An enhanced flooded battery (EFB) is a flooded battery built for start-stop. It has better deep-cycle life than a plain flooded battery but costs less than AGM. Start-stop needs many engine restarts, so the battery cycles more.

items: Use the specified type: AGM charging voltages differ from flooded.
Never open a VRLA battery; its valve is a safety device, not a service cap.

sections.h3: Battery versions, substitutes and special cases

blocks.text: Starter batteries come in several versions. The conventional flooded battery with lead-antimony grids needs topping-up. The low-maintenance and maintenance-free flooded batteries use lead-calcium grids. The enhanced flooded battery (EFB) and the AGM battery serve start-stop cars, and the gel battery, with the acid set into a gel by silica, resists deep cycling. Heavy-duty batteries for trucks, buses and tractors have thicker plates and plates fixed against vibration, and deep-cycle batteries for caravans and boats are built to be discharged far more often than a starter battery.

A substitute (replacement) battery must match the original in voltage, technology, size and terminal layout, and its CCA and Ah must be at least the original values. An AGM battery is replaced only by an AGM battery, because its charging voltage and its gas recombination differ; on cars with a battery sensor the new battery must be registered so that charging is set for a new one. Lithium-iron-phosphate 12 V starter batteries and supercapacitor packs exist as substitutes in racing and some new vehicles, but they need a matching charging strategy.

Special cases include vehicles that stand for long periods (fit a battery isolator or a maintenance charger, because standby loads drain the battery), hot climates (water loss and grid corrosion rise with temperature, so maintenance-free types and a lower charging voltage help), very cold climates (choose by CCA), and two-battery systems that keep a starter battery separate from a supply battery.

figure.caption: The reserve-capacity test of the worked example at 25 A: a battery that meets its 100 min rating reaches 10.5 V at 100 min; battery B gets there after 72 min, having delivered only 30 Ah.

spec.aria: Two discharge curves at 25 A on a voltage-time plot: the good battery stays above 10.5 V until 100 minutes; battery B falls to 10.5 V at 72 minutes.

examples.question: A battery is rated 60 Ah at the 20 h rate. (a) Find the constant current for the 20 h test. (b) The battery delivers 45 Ah before reaching 10.5 V. Find the capacity retained as a percentage.
steps: At the 20 h rate, I = Ah ÷ 20 h = 60 Ah ÷ 20 h = 3 A.
Capacity retained = delivered Ah ÷ rated Ah × 100 = 45 Ah ÷ 60 Ah × 100 = 75%.
examples.answer: The 20 h test current is 3 A, and the battery retains 75% of its rated capacity.
examples.check:
ah = 60.0
hours = 20.0
current = ah / hours
delivered = 45.0
retained = delivered / ah * 100.0
print(current)
print(retained)

examples.question: Two 12 V batteries are rated CCA 450 A and reserve capacity 100 min. (a) In a load test at half the CCA for 15 s, battery A falls from 12.6 V to 10.1 V and battery B from 12.6 V to 9.2 V. Find the load current and the internal resistance of each, and say which passes (limit 9.6 V). (b) In a reserve-capacity test at 25 A, battery B reaches 10.5 V after 72 min. Find the charge it delivered and its reserve capacity as a percentage of the rating.
steps: Load test current: I = CCA ÷ 2 = 450 A ÷ 2 = 225 A.
Battery A: drop = 12.6 V − 10.1 V = 2.5 V, so R = 2.5 V ÷ 225 A = 0.0111 Ω = 11.1 mΩ. 10.1 V is above 9.6 V: it passes.
Battery B: drop = 12.6 V − 9.2 V = 3.4 V, so R = 3.4 V ÷ 225 A = 0.0151 Ω = 15.1 mΩ. 9.2 V is below 9.6 V: it fails.
Reserve test of B: charge delivered Q = I × t = 25 A × (72 ÷ 60) h = 30 Ah.
A battery that meets its rating delivers 25 A × (100 ÷ 60) h = 41.7 Ah in the same test.
Percentage of rated reserve capacity = 72 min ÷ 100 min × 100 = 72 %.
examples.answer: The test current is 225 A; battery A (11.1 mΩ, 10.1 V) passes and battery B (15.1 mΩ, 9.2 V) fails. B delivered 30 Ah in 72 min, only 72 % of its rated reserve capacity, so it should be replaced.

traps: Ah is stored charge, not starting current; CCA is the cold-current rating.
CCA is measured at −18 °C, not room temperature; CA is at 0 °C.
Reserve capacity is in minutes, not Ah; it is measured at 25 A to 10.5 V.
Open-circuit voltage must be read after rest; a surface charge after charging gives a false high.
Do not discharge an AGM battery below about 10.5 V during a load test (and never open a VRLA battery); deep discharge shortens its life.

quiz.a: Current at −18 °C for 30 s while terminals stay at or above 7.2 V.

quiz.q: Why is reserve capacity given in minutes rather than Ah?
quiz.a: It states survival time for essential loads at a fixed 25 A to 10.5 V; minutes directly answer how long the vehicle can run without the alternator.

quiz.q: An 80 Ah battery at the 20 h rate is discharged at constant current. Find the test current.
A battery has RC = 120 min. How much charge does that represent at 25 A?
quiz.a: 25 A × 2 h = 50 Ah, but RC is quoted in minutes; do not label it Ah.

quiz.q: A battery reads 12.6 V OCV but fails a load test. Explain.
quiz.a: Surface charge or a high-resistance cell can give a good rest voltage; load test draws current and exposes weak plates or poor connections.

quiz.q: What does gas recombination do in an AGM battery?
quiz.a: Oxygen from the positive plate reaches the negative plate and recombines to water, reducing water loss.

quiz.q: Why does a start-stop vehicle need EFB or AGM rather than a plain flooded battery?
quiz.a: Frequent restarts and deeper cycling need better cycle life and charge acceptance; plain flooded loses water and ages faster.

beyond: Not for the exam. Battery management systems in electric vehicles estimate state of charge and state of health by combining voltage, current and temperature; battery sensing is a sensors topic. Standards such as SAE J537 and IEC 60095 define test methods. Search for 'VRLA recombination efficiency', 'AGM stratification' and 'battery conductance testing'.
